Position and Location:
📍 Position and Location 📍

Let's learn how to describe exactly where things are in the world!

The Ball is between the Star and the Box!

1. Learning Objectives

  • Explain position and location.
  • Describe where an object is in relation to another object.
  • Use words such as near, far, between, beside and inside.

2. What are Position and Location?

Position tells us where something is compared to a reference point or another object.

Location tells us where a person, place, or object can be found.

3. The Magic of Position Words

We use special words to help people find things without needing a measuring tape!

Position WordWhat it meansExample
NearA short distance awayThe chair is near the desk.
FarA long distance awayThe park is far from the school.
BesideAt the side of somethingThe bag is beside the chair.
BetweenIn the space separating two thingsThe ball is between the boxes.
InsideWithin somethingThe pencil is inside the case.

4. The Reference Point

A reference point is an object we use to describe where something else is. If someone asks, "Where is the slide?" you could say, "It is beside the tree." The tree is your reference point! Without a reference point, saying "It is over there" isn't very helpful.
Left, Right, Above and Below:
⬆️ Left, Right, Above and Below ⬇️

Let's master the language of moving around!

1. Learning Objectives

  • Identify left and right.
  • Describe objects as above or below other objects.
  • Understand why a person's viewpoint matters.

2. Understanding Left and Right

Left and right describe positions across your body. Your left is the side with your left hand, and your right is the side with your right hand. On a piece of paper or map, Left is usually towards the start of a written sentence, and Right is towards the end!

3. Understanding Above and Below

Above means at a higher position than something else (like a bird flying above a tree).
Below means at a lower position (like your shoes below a shelf).

4. Why Viewpoint Matters

Left and right can change depending on which way a person is facing! If you and your friend are facing each other, your right hand will be directly across from their left hand.

⚠️ Important: When looking at a map or a grid on a page, always assume Left is the left side of the page and Right is the right side of the page, unless told otherwise!
Direction and Movement:
🧭 Direction and Movement 🧭

Become a navigator by learning the compass directions!

1. Learning Objectives

  • Identify the four main directions (North, South, East, West).
  • Describe movement using directional words.
  • Explain how a starting position and direction determine a destination.

2. The Four Main Directions

The four main geographic directions are North, South, East, and West. A great way to remember them in order (going clockwise) is: Never Eat Soggy Waffles!

On a standard map:

  • North is towards the top.
  • South is towards the bottom.
  • East is towards the right.
  • West is towards the left.

3. Movement Words

We describe how objects move using special words:

  • Forward: Moving in the direction you are facing.
  • Backward: Moving opposite to the direction you are facing.
  • Turn: Changing the direction you are facing.

🤖 Robot Example: If a robot faces North and moves forward 3 steps, it travels North 3 steps!
Using Simple Maps and Grids:
🗺️ Using Simple Maps and Grids 🗺️

Learn how to find treasure (or just the library) using grids!

1. Learning Objectives

  • Understand what maps and grids are used for.
  • Read rows and columns on a grid.
  • Use a map key and cell references to find places.

2. What is a Grid?

A grid is a pattern of horizontal rows and vertical columns. It divides a map into smaller squares (called cells) to make places incredibly easy to find!

  • Columns go up and down (vertical). They are usually labeled with letters (A, B, C).
  • Rows go left and right (horizontal). They are usually labeled with numbers (1, 2, 3).

3. Finding the Cell Reference

To find where something is on a grid, you combine the Column letter and the Row number! In the picture above:

  • The Tree (🌳) is in Column B, Row 1. Its cell reference is B1.
  • The House (🏠) is in A2.
  • The Star (⭐) is in C2.

4. Map Keys (Legends)

A map key or legend is a little box on a map that explains what the tiny pictures (symbols) mean. For example, it might tell you that 🌳 stands for "Park" and 🏠 stands for "School". Always read the key so you don't confuse a swimming pool with a lake!
Turns and Rotations:
🔄 Turns and Rotations 🔄

Get ready to spin! Let's measure how much things turn.

1. Learning Objectives

  • Understand what a turn and a rotation mean.
  • Recognise quarter-turns, half-turns, and full turns.
  • Distinguish clockwise from anticlockwise.

2. Clockwise vs. Anticlockwise

A turn changes the direction you are facing. A rotation is a turning movement around a fixed point.

  • Clockwise: Turning in the exact same direction that the hands of a clock move (to the right).
  • Anticlockwise (or Counter-clockwise): Turning in the opposite direction of a clock (to the left).

3. Types of Turns

We measure turns in fractions of a circle or in degrees (°). A full circle is 360°.

Name of TurnDegreesWhat happens?
Quarter-Turn90°You face the side (like turning from North to East).
Half-Turn180°You face the exact opposite direction (like turning from North to South).
Full Turn360°You spin all the way around and face the same way you started!

⭐ Math Tip: If you face West and do a half-turn (180°), you will always face East, no matter if you spun clockwise or anticlockwise!
Describing Routes:
🚶‍♂️ Describing Routes 🚶‍♀️

Step-by-step instructions to get from Start to Finish!

1. Learning Objectives

  • Explain what a route is.
  • Describe a journey using clear movement instructions.
  • Follow a sequence of instructions from a starting point to a destination.

2. What is a Route?

A route is the specific path taken to travel from one place to another. Giving someone a route is like giving a robot a list of code to follow.

3. Route Vocabulary

  • Start: Where the journey begins.
  • Destination: Where the journey ends.
  • Go Straight: Move forward without turning.
  • Grid Space: One block or "step" on a map.

4. Writing Clear Instructions

To guide the robot (🤖) to the finish flag (🏁) on the grid above, we must give it a sequence of orders in the exact right order. If we mess up the order, the robot will crash!

  1. Start at the Robot.
  2. Move 1 grid space East (Right).
  3. Move 1 grid space North (Up).
  4. Move 2 grid spaces East (Right).
  5. Stop at the Destination!
Ordered Pairs — Introductory:
📍 Ordered Pairs (Introductory) 📍

The secret code of coordinate grids: (x, y)!

1. Learning Objectives

  • Understand what an ordered pair is.
  • Recognise the two numbers in an ordered pair.
  • Understand why the order of the numbers matters!

2. What is an Ordered Pair?

An ordered pair is a pair of numbers written in brackets, separated by a comma. It tells you exactly where a point lives on a grid. We write it as (x, y).

  • The first number (x): Tells you how far to move horizontally (left/right).
  • The second number (y): Tells you how far to move vertically (up/down).

3. The Origin

Every grid has a starting point called the Origin. Its coordinates are always (0, 0). It is the very bottom-left corner where the two axis lines meet. You always start counting from the Origin!

4. Why does the Order matter?

Order is incredibly important! The point (2, 4) means "Go right 2, and up 4."
But the point (4, 2) means "Go right 4, and up 2."
They use the same numbers, but they land on completely different spots on the map! Always remember: Walk down the hallway (x) before you take the stairs (y)!
Plotting Points on a Grid:
✏️ Plotting Points on a Grid ✏️

Grab your pencil, it's time to mark the map!

1. Learning Objectives

  • Identify the horizontal and vertical axes on a grid.
  • Read coordinates written as (x, y).
  • Plot points accurately on a coordinate grid.

2. What does Plotting mean?

Plotting a point means drawing a small dot exactly where a set of coordinates tells you to on a grid.

  • x-axis: The flat, horizontal line at the bottom.
  • y-axis: The tall, vertical line going up the side.

3. How to Plot a Point

Let's plot the point (3, 2), exactly like the picture above!

  1. Start at the Origin (0,0) in the bottom left corner.
  2. Read the first number (x). It is 3. Move your finger 3 lines to the right.
  3. Read the second number (y). It is 2. Move your finger 2 lines up.
  4. Draw your dot right where the two grid lines cross! Don't forget to write "(3, 2)" next to it as a label!

4. Watch out for Zero!

If you see a zero in the coordinates, it means "don't move!"
The point (0, 4) means move right 0, and up 4. The dot will be drawn directly on the y-axis line!
First-Quadrant Coordinates:
➕ First-Quadrant Coordinates ➕

Welcome to Quadrant I, where everything is positive!

1. Learning Objectives

  • Understand what a quadrant is.
  • Identify the first quadrant on a coordinate grid.
  • Recognise positive x and y coordinates.

2. What is a Quadrant?

If you draw a giant plus sign (+), it divides space into four different squares. In maths, we call these squares Quadrants. They are numbered with Roman numerals (I, II, III, IV) going in a circle anticlockwise.

3. The Magic of Quadrant I

In primary school, we spend almost all our time in the top-right square, known as the First Quadrant (Quadrant I).

Why is it special? Because in the First Quadrant, every single number is positive (greater than zero)!

If you see a coordinate like (4, 5), you instantly know it lives in Quadrant I because both numbers are positive.

4. Comparing Points

If you plot two points in the first quadrant, you can easily compare them:

  • Point A is (2, 5) and Point B is (6, 5). Point B is further to the right because its x-coordinate is bigger (6 > 2).
  • Point C is (3, 2) and Point D is (3, 8). Point D is much higher up because its y-coordinate is bigger (8 > 2).
Patterns on Coordinate Grids:
📈 Patterns on Coordinate Grids 📈

Connect the dots to find the hidden mathematical rules!

1. Learning Objectives

  • Recognise patterns in coordinate pairs.
  • Identify how points move across a grid.
  • Predict the next point in a sequence.

2. What is a Coordinate Pattern?

A coordinate pattern is a sequence of points that follows a specific math rule. If you plot them on a grid, they usually make a perfectly straight line!

3. Three Types of Patterns

  • ➡️ Horizontal Pattern: The points move flat to the right. The x-coordinate increases, but the y-coordinate stays exactly the same.
    Example: (1, 3), (2, 3), (3, 3).
  • ⬆️ Vertical Pattern: The points go straight up. The x-coordinate stays the same, but the y-coordinate increases.
    Example: (2, 1), (2, 2), (2, 3).
  • ↗️ Diagonal Pattern: The points go up and to the right! Both coordinates change.
    Example: (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3).

4. Predicting the Next Point

Look at the sequence in the picture above: (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3). What is the yellow mystery dot?

To solve it, act like a detective and look at the numbers separately:

  1. Look at the first numbers (x): 1, 2, 3... The rule is "Add 1". So the next x is 4.
  2. Look at the second numbers (y): 1, 2, 3... The rule is also "Add 1". So the next y is 4.

The next point in the pattern is (4, 4)!
